newsitem.title: UK: UK stocks end roller-coaster day down on Dow slide.
newsitem.headline: UK stocks end roller-coaster day down on Dow slide.

text.p: UK shares ended a volatile session sharply lower as Wall Street plunged during London trading hours on fears that U.S. blue chips may be overpriced and due for a correction, dealers and strategists said.
The FTSE 100 index dropped 53.2 points or 1.3 percent to 3,982.5, after rising 72 points the previous two sessions.
The key index had been down nearly 2.0 percent or 73 points after Wall Street plunged over 100 points in the first two hours of trade in New York.
"We didn't get a meltdown today but we're not out of the woods yet," said Kirit Shah, strategist at Sanwa International.
"If the Japanese reduce their holdings in U.S. assets and (U.S. Treasury) bond yields head higher the Dow could fall sharply," Shah added. The Dow industrials average was down 85 points by 1630 GMT.
Market participants have been worried for several weeks that the Dow, which has jumped nearly 30 percent this year, could be headed for a large downward correction.
Those fears were exacerbated on Wednesday by press reports that Japanese investors may be on the verge of reducing their holdings in U.S. dollar assets, particularly U.S. Treasury bonds.
Because of the uncertainty, Shah expected the FTSE to remain volatile in the run-up to Christmas and saw only a limited potential for share prices to rise in the short-term.
"Ahead of Christmas I see the roller-coaster ride continuing," he said. With the prospect of rising UK interest rates, there is really not that much upside for the FTSE," Shah added.

The FTSE's recent gyrations began last Friday, when the FTSE plunged 88 points after U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan said U.S. stock prices were overstretched, hinting that U.S. rates might need to increase to stem the rise.
But the market clawed back most of those losses on Monday and Tuesday only to see the FTSE surrender a large portion of the recovery on Wednesday.

"With volatility like this, a lot of institutions will decide not to get involved so we could see volumes drop in the run up to Christmas," the head of trading and a large brokerage said. "Basically, we're just going to watch Wall Street and wait. If it crashes, we'll go with it," he added.
"The only consolation is that since we haven't risen as much this year as Wall Street, we probably won't fall as far", the trader said.
The FTSE 100 has risen by around nine percent in 1996, one third of the Dow's rate.

Over the near-term, the FTSE has some support at the 3,960-3,963 levels, with resistance at 3,995-4,000, technical analysts said. A drop below 3,960 should herald further weakness to the next major support at 3,885-3,900.
UK gilts lost ground, tracking weak U.S. Treasuries and bunds. More downward pressure is expected on Thursday, dealers said.
The benchmark March long gilt future closed at 109-09, down 28/32.
FTSE 100 decliners outpaced advancers by nearly nine to one, in a trading volume of around 770 million shares by 1630 GMT.
Burmah Castrol shrugged off the general market gloom, rising 21-1/2p at 10.85 stg as a fall in the price of crude oil prompted traders to cover short positions in the stock, dealers said.
Imperial Tobacco inched 1p higher to close at 379-1/2 amid renewed takeover speculation. B.A.T Industries, seen as a possible suitor, ended 2-1/2p higher at 490-1/2.
-- Dale Faulken, London Newroom +44 171 542 7717
